title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 336
paragraphs: After Proteus, they told me, Rhampsinitos succeeded to the kingdom, and he left as his memorial the gateway to the temple of Hephaistos that faces westward. In front of the gateway he set up two statues, each twenty-five cubits tall. The Egyptians call the one on the north side Summer, and the one on the south side Winter; to Summer they pay reverence and make offerings, while to Winter they do the opposite. (a) This king, they said, gained great wealth in silver, more than any king born after him could match or even approach. Wishing to keep his treasure safe, he had a stone chamber built, with one of its walls forming part of the outside of his palace. The builder, however, had a design upon it, and he contrived as follows: he set one of the stones in such a way that it could easily be removed from the wall by two men, or even by a single man. So when the chamber was finished and the king stored his money inside it, the builder, after some time, drawing near the end of his life, called his two sons to him. He told them how he had arranged the matter when building the king's treasury, all in forethought for them, so that they might have ample means of living. He gave them the precise measurements for removing the stone, telling them that if they paid heed to this, they would be the stewards of the king's treasury. Then he died, and his sons made no long delay in setting to work. They went to the palace by night, found the stone in the wall of the chamber, dealt with it easily, and carried away a great quantity of the wealth within. (b) When the king happened to open the chamber, he was astonished to see the vessels falling short of their full amount, and he did not know whom to blame, since the seals were unbroken and the chamber had been shut close. But when, on opening the chamber a second time and a third, the money was each time seen to be diminished — for the thieves did not slacken in their assaults — he did as follows. He had traps made and set them around the vessels in which the money was kept; and when the thieves came as before and one of them entered, as soon as he came near a vessel he was caught fast in the trap. Realizing how desperate his case was, he immediately called his brother, showed him what had happened, and bade him climb in as quickly as possible and cut off his head, lest he be seen and recognized, bringing destruction upon his brother as well. To the other this seemed sound advice, and he was persuaded; he did so, and fitting the stone back into its place, he departed home carrying his brother's head with him. (c) When day came, the king entered the chamber and was utterly amazed to see the body of the thief held in the trap without its head, the chamber unbroken, and no way to come in or go out. Being at a loss, he hung the dead body up on the wall and set guards there, with orders to seize anyone seen weeping or lamenting and bring him before the king. When the body had been hung up, the mother was deeply grieved. Speaking with her surviving son, she ordered him to contrive, by whatever means he could, to take down and bring home the body of his dead brother; and if he failed to do this, she earnestly threatened that she would go and inform the king that he had the money. (d) Since the mother dealt harshly with the surviving son, and he could not persuade her with his many arguments, he contrived a device for his purpose. He provided himself with asses, filled some skins with wine, loaded them upon the asses, and drove them along. When he came opposite to those guarding the corpse, he pulled out two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied. As the wine ran out, he began to beat his head and cry out loudly, as if he did not know which of the asses to turn to first. When the guards saw the wine flowing out in streams, they ran together onto the road with drinking vessels in their hands and collected the wine that was spilling, counting it pure gain. He railed at them all violently, pretending to be angry, and when the guards tried to appease him, after a while he feigned to be pacified and to abate his anger. At last he drove his asses out of the road and began to set their loads right. Then more talk arose among them, one or two of them made jokes at him and brought him to laugh with them, and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins as well. At that they lay down then and there without further ado, intending to drink, and they took him into their company and invited him to stay with them and join them in their drinking. So he, as one might expect, was persuaded and stayed. As they welcomed him in friendly fashion as they drank, he made them a present of another skin. So at length, having drunk liberally, the guards became completely drunk, and being overcome by sleep they went to bed on the very spot where they had been drinking. He then, since it was now far on in the night, first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards. After that he placed the dead body upon the asses and drove them home, having accomplished what his mother had enjoined upon him. (e) When it was reported to the king that the dead body of the thief had been stolen away, he displayed great anger; and desiring above all to find out who it could be that devised these things, he did this — so at least they said, though I do not believe the account. He caused his own daughter to sit in a brothel and ordered her to receive all comers equally, and before lying with any of them she was to compel each one to tell her what was the most cunning and the most unholy deed he had done in all his life; and whoever should relate what had happened concerning the thief, she must seize him and not let him go. So she did as her father had enjoined. The thief, hearing the purpose for which this was done and wishing to outdo the king in cleverness, did this. From the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his cloak. Having gone in to the king's daughter and being asked the same question as the others, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother caught in a trap in the king's treasure-chamber, and the most cunning deed when he made the guards drunk and took down the dead body of his brother that had been hung up. When she heard this and tried to lay hold of him, the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse, which she grasped and held, thinking she was holding the man's own arm. But the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. (f) When this also was reported to the king, he was at first amazed at the ready invention and daring of the fellow. Then afterwards he sent round to all the cities and made proclamation, granting a free pardon to the thief and promising a great reward as well if he would come into his presence. The thief, trusting to the proclamation, came to the king, and Rhampsinitos marvelled greatly at him and gave him this daughter of his to wife, considering him to be the most knowing of all men. For just as the Egyptians were distinguished from all other men, so was he distinguished from the other Egyptians.
